title: Missing-Field Scan — Core Method
description: The completeness analyzer compares every record against the expected schema and lists which required fields are absent, per record and in aggregate. A field missing from 2% of records is noise; missing from 40% signals a systematic ingestion failure. The scan distinguishes 'field absent' from 'field present but empty', because the remedies differ. This is the first and most basic completeness check, and it catches the most problems. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Broken-Reference Check — Core Method
description: Records point at each other, and pointers rot: the target is deleted, the ID is mistyped, the namespace changes. The analyzer resolves every reference in the archive and reports the dangling ones with the source record and the dead target. Dangling-reference rates are tracked over time, because a rising rate means an upstream deletion process is not cleaning up after itself. Referential integrity is what makes an archive a web of knowledge instead of a pile of pages. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Empty-Record Detection — Core Method
description: Some records exist but say nothing — no fields beyond the ID, or fields all null. The empty-record detector scores records by filled-field count and flags those below threshold, separating true empties from sparse-but-valid records. Empty records usually trace to failed ingestions or placeholder rows that were never filled. Finding them lets the archive either complete them or remove the husks honestly. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Schema Coverage Check — Core Method
description: Coverage asks the reverse question: for each field in the schema, what fraction of records actually populate it? Fields with near-zero coverage are dead weight — deprecated, misnamed, or never implemented. The analyzer reports coverage per field per record type, because a field can be vital for one type and meaningless for another. Coverage below an agreed threshold triggers either a fill effort or a schema cleanup. This keeps schemas honest about what the archive really holds. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
recs = [{"a": 1, "b": 2}, {"a": 3}, {"a": 4, "b": 5}]
fields = ["a", "b"]
for f in fields:
    cov = sum(1 for r in recs if f in r) / len(recs)
    print("field %r coverage %.0f%%" % (f, 100 * cov))

title: Severity-Ranked Gap Report — Core Method
description: Findings are useless without prioritization, so the analyzer ranks every gap by severity: broken references in core collections outrank missing optional fields in obscure ones. Severity combines the gap type, the affected record count, and the collection's importance weight. The report lists gaps highest-severity-first with concrete remediation steps — re-ingest, backfill, or deprecate. A ranked gap report turns completeness from an abstract worry into a work queue. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
gaps = [("missing date", 400, 1), ("broken ref", 12, 10), ("empty rec", 3, 5)]
ranked = sorted(gaps, key=lambda g: -(g[1] * g[2]))
for name, n, sev in ranked:
    print("%-12s count=%4d severity=%d score=%d" % (name, n, sev, n * sev))
